patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v1] fuse: don't launder folios of a bad inode

version_history.subject: [PATCH v1] fuse: don't launder folios of a bad inode

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the fuse file system where dirty pages are not properly handled when an inode is marked bad. The fix involves checking if the inode is bad before attempting to write back dirty data, and returning -EIO if it is.

review_comments.author: Horst Birthelmer
review_comments.summary: Identified the bug as not having hit their test cases, but approved the fix and added Reviewed-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Oct 06, 2026 at 03:51:36AM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> fuse_flush() and fuse_writepages() reject writing back dirty data for
> any inode that has been marked bad, but fuse_launder_folio() doesn't.
> 
> This can cause the following warning in fuse_write_file_get() to
> trigger, as reported by syzbot:
> 
> WARNING: fs/fuse/file.c:2043 at fuse_write_file_get fs/fuse/file.c:2043 [inline]
> WARNING: fs/fuse/file.c:2043 at fuse_iomap_writeback_range+0x7c8/0x18f0 fs/fuse/file.c:2227
> Call Trace:
>     iomap_writeback_folio+0x1526/0x2490 fs/iomap/buffered-io.c:2022
>     fuse_launder_folio+0x17b/0x240 fs/fuse/file.c:2331
>     folio_unmap_invalidate+0x4cd/0x830 mm/truncate.c:634
>     invalidate_inode_pages2_range+0x629/0xb30 mm/truncate.c:726
>     fuse_open+0x5a6/0x770 fs/fuse/file.c:297
> 
> This can be hit on a writeback cache mount:
> 1) a writeable file is open and a buffered write dirties some pages
> 2) another thread opens the same file read-only. fuse_open() passes the
>    bad inode check and sends OPEN to the server.
> 3) a SETATTR reply with the wrong file type marks the inode bad
> 4) the writeable file is closed. Flush and release skip writeback
>    because the inode is bad. The pages stay dirty but the file gets
>    removed from write_files.
> 5) server replies to the OPEN. The reply has no FOPEN_KEEP_CACHE, so
>    fuse_open() calls invalidate_inode_pages2().
> 6) the invalidation finds the dirty pages and calls
>    fuse_launder_folio(), which finds no wriable file and hits the
>    WARN_ON in fuse_write_file_get().
> 
> Instead of trying to write back dirty data for the bad inode,
> fuse_launder_folio() should return -EIO.
> 
> Fixes: 5d069dbe8aaf ("fuse: fix bad inode")
> Reported-by: syzbot+e8200299b0556976e13c@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
> Closes: https://syzkaller.appspot.com/bug?extid=e8200299b0556976e13c
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> ---
>  fs/fuse/file.c | 3 +++
>  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
> 
> diff --git a/fs/fuse/file.c b/fs/fuse/file.c
> index 6d707f2b3bff..0ef46f6e0267 100644
> --- a/fs/fuse/file.c
> +++ b/fs/fuse/file.c
> @@ -2351,6 +2351,9 @@ static int fuse_launder_folio(struct folio *folio)
>  		.wb_ctx	= &data,
>  	};
>  
> +	if (fuse_is_bad(wpc.inode))
> +		return -EIO;
> +
>  	if (folio_clear_dirty_for_io(folio)) {
>  		err = iomap_writeback_folio(&wpc, folio);
>  		err = fuse_iomap_writeback_submit(&wpc, err);
> -- 
> 2.52.0
> 
> 

Hi Joanne,

I have tested a lot of notification invalidation lately.
Did not hit this one yet.

LGTM!

Feel free to add

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/3] mm: memcontrol: factor reclaim logic out of try_charge_memcg()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the reclaim logic in try_charge_memcg() into two helper functions: memcg_charge_may_reclaim() and memcg_charge_reclaim(). The goal is to make it easier for subsequent patches to reuse this logic. No functional changes are made.

review_comments.author: Rik van Riel
review_comments.summary: Identified the cleanup as nice and applied the Reviewed-by tag.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/3] mm: memcontrol: add mem_cgroup_reclaim_for_batch()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, mem_cgroup_reclaim_for_batch(), which allows callers to reclaim memory from a memory cgroup in batches instead of one folio at a time. This is useful for callers that charge a batch of folios one at a time, such as readahead, and can trigger multiple reclaim passes when the memory cgroup limit is reached. The function retries reclaim only once if it fails, making it suitable for callers that are okay with charges failing. The patch also adds a new function to internal.h to provide a default implementation for non-MEMCG configurations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 3/3] mm/readahead: avoid per-folio memcg reclaim
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the readahead mechanism to avoid per-folio memory cgroup (memcg) reclaim, which was causing livelocks and high CPU usage on systems with many tasks faulting in the same cgroup. Instead of charging each folio separately, the patch adds multiple folios to the page cache at once without direct reclaim, and only reclaims for the rest of the window when the memcg is at its limit. If the memcg hits its limit again before adding all folios, it attempts one more time. If there's still no room, readahead stops early rather than trying harder. This change affects only speculative readahead folios and does not alter behavior for actual fault or read requests.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in Linux's readahead mechanism by avoiding per-folio memory cgroup (memcg) reclaim. When multiple tasks fault in the same cgroup, the frequent per-folio charges trigger reclaim, leading to livelocks and high CPU usage. The patches modify readahead to charge all folios in its window at once when the memcg is at its limit, reducing the number of reclaim passes by 94-96% and eliminating livelocks on a test system with btrfs file systems and compress-force=zstd:3.

review_comments.author: Jan Kara
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Jan Kara noted that the patch does not handle the case where a folio is already mapped in another memcg, which could lead to incorrect reclaim behavior and requested additional checks to ensure correct handling of such cases.

Jan Kara questioned whether the folios being faulted are actually used before they get reclaimed, suggesting that if not, it would be more efficient to stop reading them in the first place.
sentiment_signals: questioning the effectiveness of the patch
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Joanne!

On Fri 02-10-26 17:15:52, Joanne Koong wrote:

---

I cannot really comment on how much sense this makes from memcg POV (I'll
defer to people understanding that area better). When I'm reading your
problem description I'm wondering about one thing: Are the folios we are
faulting around really used in your workloads before they get reclaimed?
Because what I'd expect to happen in cases under heavy memory pressure is
that ra->mmap_miss would quickly grow over the limit (100) and we'd just
stop doing mmap readahead for the files. If the read-around pages aren't
getting used before being evicted, then the first natural thing would be to
actually stop reading them in the first place :) The mmap_miss logic is
actually rather dumb so I wouldn't be surprised if it doesn't work in your
case...

The experiments you have conducted below indicate that if you effectively
disable readahead you get more page faults & smaller IO requests (expected)
but for your realistic loads under memory pressure is that really an
overall performance loss?

								Honza

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that the swapoff path needs to drop the per-vswap spinlock before calling try_to_unmap(), agreed to restructure in v2, and clarified that this change is necessary for avoiding memcg reclaim

Author Joanne Koong is addressing a concern about the high rate of reclaim triggered by mmap readaround in btrfs file systems due to large ra_pages settings, which causes most faults to land on already cached pages. She suggests computing the mmap readaround size differently, either with a fixed cap or dynamically adapting the window based on usage.

The author is addressing concerns about the accuracy of mmap_miss counting, specifically that it overcounts hits and doesn't account for wasted pages. They suggest changing the count to track pages read vs pages used instead, or alternatively getting information from reclaim. The author believes these improvements would be complementary to their original patch rather than a replacement.

Author addressed a concern about the impact of removing read-around on sequential readers, suggesting that it would have a minimal effect on random-access workloads but potentially harm sequential readers.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Jan!

Thanks for taking a look at this.

On Mon, Oct 5, 2026 at 2:27 PM Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz> wrote:

---

I ran some traces on two production hosts and am roughly seeing:
* of the readahead folios that reclaim dropped during runs, ~66-78%
had never been mapped
* running a 60 second sample: mmap read-around accounts for ~86% of
readahead on both hosts. 77% of the folios it adds are never mapped.
Around 10-15% are faulted on directly and the rest are mapped by
fault-around. mmap_miss skipped read-around for only ~2-4% of major
faults. For faults that triggered read-around, mmap_miss was below 10
for 74%-96% of them.

This looks specific to mmap-readaround though. On these same hosts,
I'm seeing much better utilization by buffered read readaheads (only
~30% never accessed).

I think a big part of what's causing this is that btrfs by default
sets ra_pages to at least 4M (in open_ctree() in fs/btrfs/disk-io.c).
In do_sync_mmap_readahead(), I see "ra->size = ra->ra_pages;". So it
looks like mmap uses this same value directly for how many pages to
read-around (with 4M ra_pages, this is 1024 pages), even if the faults
are random accesses. I think this also accounts for why mmap_miss is
so low too, since with the readaround windows that large, most faults
land on pages that are already in the page cache, and each of those
minor faults count as up to 16 hits, while each major fault only adds
one miss and happens a lot less frequently. With many processes
mapping the same file, I think it makes the problem worse (eg each
process has minor faults to map it to its page tables, but there was
only 1 major fault to load it into the cache).
(Adding the btrfs list to cc. Apologies for not doing this from the
beginning. The full thread is at
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/20261003001555.3498357-1-joannelkoong@gmail.com/).

Instead of having the mmap readaround size coupled 1:1 with ra_pages,
do you think it makes sense to compute it differently? Like either
having some sort of fixed cap (readaround never bigger than
VM_READAHEAD_PAGES) or dynamically adapting the window where it starts
small and grows if/when readaround folios get used and shrinking when
they don't? I don't think this would degrade sequential mmap access
(eg async readahead would ramp the window back up to ra_pages in a few
steps once the fault hits the PG_readahead marker) and I think it
could be beneficial in general too, as less pages need to get read in
speculatively that wouldn't be used, which would also lead to less
reclaim.

---

Do you think it'd be better to have mmap_miss count pages read vs
pages used instead of counting misses and hits seen at fault time? I
think the problem we're running into here at Meta which mmap_miss is
not detecting is that there's lots of wasted pages that never reach a
fault. It also seems to overcount hits, eg a single fault can subtract
mmap_miss by up to 16 if there are nearby cached pages (which might
have been cached by buffered reads, not mmap), even if those cached
pages never actually get touched. And the same cached page can be
counted as a hit several times, once for each process that minor
faults it in. Or maybe there's some simple way to get the info from
reclaim instead? Where if reclaim is evicting a readahead page that
was never accessed, that's counted as a miss? imo that seems a lot
more accurate as a signal though that also seems a lot more invasive,
like needing a new page flag.

As I understand it, both these improvements (detangling mmap
readaround size from ra_pages and improving mmap_miss heuristics)
would be complementary to this series rather than a replacement for
the per-folio reclaim fix. Does this match your view?

---

I haven't measured end-to-end performance for that on production loads
but my suspicion is that losing read-around at the memcg limit
wouldn't affect random-access workloads like these much, while it
would for sequential readers.

Thanks,
Joanne

[PATCH v2] mm: page_alloc: make defrag_mode retries follow the promoted order

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of page allocation in defrag_mode to make retries follow the promoted order, rather than the original request order. This change is intended to prevent indefinite retrying by requests that are not movable, which can lead to high memory pressure and OOM killing. The patch also updates the retry logic for direct reclaim and compaction to take into account the promoted order, and resets the retry counters when a fallback attempt is made. As a result of this change, the number of should_reclaim_retry() calls and peak memory pressure are significantly reduced, leading to improved system performance.

On (26/10/06 11:47), Nhat Pham wrote:
> On Tue, Oct 6, 2026 at 2:23\u202fAM Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:
> >
> > Stores and loads serialize on the same per-CPU acomp request and mutex.
> > A low-priority store can be preempted as soon as the compressor drops
> > its stream lock, while it still holds the mutex. A higher-priority load
> > on that CPU then waits until the store runs again, which can take a
> > long time when other tasks are runnable.
> >
> > Give compression and decompression their own request, completion wait
> > and mutex. Since commit e2c3b6b21c77f ("mm: zswap: use SG list
> > decompression APIs from zsmalloc"), the per-CPU buffer is only used for
> > compression. The two requests can share the per-CPU transform: no
> > in-tree implementation modifies transform state while (de)compressing,
> > and shared codec state has its own locking. Loads can still wait for
> > each other on the decompression mutex, and stores still serialize on
> > the compression mutex.
> >
> > This follows the proposal from Sergey Senozhatsky for the same split
> > for zram [1].

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm: zswap: use separate compression and decompression requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the compression and decompression requests in zswap, allowing them to run concurrently without waiting for each other. This is done by introducing a new struct to hold the separate requests and mutexes for each operation. The change follows a proposal from Sergey Senozhatsky for similar splitting of requests in zram. The patch aims to improve performance by reducing the time spent on compression and decompression, especially when there are multiple tasks competing for CPU resources.

series_items.patch_summary: The patch modifies the zswap decompression algorithm to use stack requests for synchronous decompression, reducing serialization and improving performance.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Identified the patch as a good solution to reduce serialization in zswap decompression. Approved the patch and added an Acked-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Oct 6, 2026 at 2:23 AM Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:
>
> With separate requests for compression and decompression, loads still
> serialize on the per-CPU decompression mutex. A low-priority load that
> is preempted after the codec drops its stream lock keeps holding the mutex
> and stalls every other load on that CPU, including higher-priority ones.
>
> Synchronous algorithms whose requests need no extra context can use an
> on-stack request, so decompress with one and take no zswap lock. All
> in-tree software compressors qualify. Asynchronous algorithms, and
> synchronous ones with request context, keep the per-CPU request and
> mutex, which is still taken before the zsmalloc read lock.
>
> Reading the per-CPU context without the mutex is safe. Since
> commit ef3c0f6cb798e ("mm: zswap: tie per-CPU acomp_ctx lifetime to the
> pool"), it is set up before its CPU comes online and is not torn down
> until the pool is destroyed. The codecs keep their own stream locks, and
> crypto_acomp_decompress() rejects on-stack requests only for
> asynchronous transforms, which never take this path.
>
> For software compressors this drops the heap request added by the
> previous patch. The on-stack request and wait take 216 bytes, which
> makes the load path about 270 bytes deeper on x86-64. Asynchronous
> algorithms pay this too.
>

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series reduces contention on loads in the zswap compression system by introducing separate requests and mutexes for compression and decompression, allowing loads to no longer wait for stores. The second patch further optimizes synchronous decompression by using on-stack requests when possible, reducing lock contention even more. This results in significant performance improvements, with reads over 10ms falling from 26-35 per run to none with a single CPU and from 3-18 per run to at most one with eight CPUs.
